title: Small Works of Power
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · Portrait, symbol and inscription
objective: Students will read a coin as a work of art that carries a message. They will identify the three elements a coin designer works with — **portrait**, **symbol** and **inscription** — and explain how the coins of the New Testament used them to declare power and belief: an emperor’s face, a pagan god, symbols chosen because a face was forbidden, and symbols chosen to provoke. They will learn how a coin was struck, read the clues that expose a fake, and design a coin of their own that says something on purpose.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Coins, flags and logos all speak before anyone reads a word. Seeing how a design makes its claim lets you read every image that asks for your attention, and make your own say what you mean.

materials: The coin images on page 3, projected or printed; the exhibition online if you have a screen
Any coin from a student’s pocket or purse, and a magnifying glass if you have one
Pencils and fine black pens; differentiated handouts, one per student
questions: Cover the inscription on the Tribute Penny with your thumb. What does the coin still say? What does it lose?
Herod’s designers could not use a face. If you had to say *king* without a face, what would you draw?
Why might a ladle or three ears of grain offend more than an emperor’s portrait?
The Temple accepted a coin with a pagan god on it because its silver was pure. What does that tell you about how people valued the image and the metal?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** the four coins of this lesson sit in Cases 6 and 7, each with a magnified view of both sides. Then play *Real or Replica?* — five pairs of ancient coins, one genuine and one fake. All of it is online too.

steps.title: The smallest public artwork
script: Hand a coin to a student and ask the class: *“Who designed this? What did they choose to put on it, and what did they leave off? Who is it trying to impress?”* Then: *“Two thousand years ago, people in Jerusalem carried coins that made claims about gods and emperors. Some designs were chosen to cause offense. Today we read them as artists.”*

steps.title: A ruler’s face
script: **A ruler’s face.** Show the Tribute Penny (a museum-quality replica). One side carries the face of the emperor Tiberius; the other reads PONTIF MAXIM — *High Priest*. The portrait says *this man rules*; the inscription claims religious authority too. Point out how the letters run around the rim and frame the image.

steps.purpose: Read a portrait and an inscription working together on one coin.
students: Find the **portrait**. Whose face is it?
Find the **inscription**. What does it claim?
How do the letters frame the picture?

steps.title: Portrait, symbol, inscription
script: **A god’s face.** Show the Shekel of Tyre (also a replica). Its face is the pagan god Melqart. The Temple accepted only this coin for its tax because its silver was so pure: the purity of the metal overrode the offensiveness of the image.
**No face at all.** Show Herod the Great’s prutah. Herod’s coins carry no human image, because Jewish law forbade it. His designers had to say *king* with symbols alone.

**Symbols that provoke.** Show Pontius Pilate’s prutah, minted in 29/30 AD. A simpulum, a Roman libation ladle, on one side; three bound ears of grain on the other. The exhibition calls both deliberately provocative pagan symbols on Jewish coinage. A symbol can be as loud as a face.

steps.title: Real or replica?
script: **How a coin is made.** A genuine ancient coin was struck between two dies, one for each side. Striking leaves crisp detail and die-stress lines; two thousand years of handling soften the high points evenly. Forgers struggle to fake those marks — which is how experts catch them (page 3).

groups.label: Lysimachus tetradrachm, from *Real or Replica?*
groups.text: Both sides of each. A genuine coin was struck between two dies; a sand-cast fake was poured into a mold made in sand.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels look at real coins, then design a coin of their own, front and back.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Label the portrait, symbol and inscription on the Tribute Penny and on Pilate’s prutah, match three words to their meanings, then design a coin with a picture on the front and words on the back.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare Herod the Great’s coin, which has no face, with the Tribute Penny, which does. Explain what each design says about its ruler, then design a coin with **no face** whose symbols carry a message.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Analyze how three coins communicate power and belief, critique a sand-cast fake from *Real or Replica?* by its visual clues, then design a coin and write an artist’s rationale for every choice.

steps.purpose: Design a coin of their own at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. Look closely at real coins, then design your own, front and back.

steps.title: Gallery walk
script: Lay the designs out as a gallery. Each student points to one choice on a classmate’s coin and says what message it sends. Close with the question the coins keep asking: *what is the smallest thing you could make that would still say who you are?*

steps.purpose: Hear what each design says, in a classmate’s words.
students: Point to one choice on a classmate’s coin.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
